## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(simling)
```

## The data {.smaller}

`rhythm_metrics` comes from a simulated study of speech rhythm. Eight speakers of each of six languages read sentences, told a story and spoke freely, and each of the 1200 speech samples has two measures we use today: the speech rate (`rate`, in syllables per second) and ΔC (`delta_c`, in ms). ΔC is the standard deviation of the durations of the consonant intervals in a sample, one of the [rhythm metrics]{.hl} that phoneticians use to compare languages.

```{r}
glimpse(rhythm_metrics)
```

Today's question: does ΔC change with speech rate?

---

## 1. Look before you fit

### 1.1 A scatterplot

Plot `delta_c` against `rate` with `geom_point()`, with speech rate on the `x` axis. Label both axes in words, with units. Do faster samples have a larger or a smaller ΔC?

::: solution

```{r scatter, eval = FALSE}
rhythm_metrics |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = delta_c)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum2", alpha = 0.3) +
  xlab("Speech rate (syllables per second)") + ylab("ΔC (ms)")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "scatter", echo = FALSE}
```

The faster the sample, the smaller ΔC tends to be. The points form a roughly straight cloud, so a line is a reasonable first model.

:::

### 1.2 Add the line

Add the [regression line]{.hl} with `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`.

::: solution

```{r scatter-line, eval = FALSE}
rhythm_metrics |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = delta_c)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum2", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  xlab("Speech rate (syllables per second)") + ylab("ΔC (ms)")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "scatter-line", echo = FALSE}
```

:::

---

## 2. Fitting the model

### 2.1 `lm()`

Fit a linear model of `delta_c` as a function of `rate` and save it as `m`. Print its coefficients with `coef()`.

::: solution

```{r}
m <- lm(delta_c ~ rate, data = rhythm_metrics)
coef(m)
```

:::

### 2.2 Read the coefficients

Complete the sentence: "With every extra syllable per second, ΔC changes by ___ ms." Then say what the [intercept]{.hl} means here. Is it a useful number?

::: solution

With every extra syllable per second, ΔC falls by `r round(abs(coef(m)["rate"]), 1)` ms.

The intercept, `r round(coef(m)[1], 1)` ms, is the predicted ΔC for a sample spoken at 0 syllables per second, that is, for no speech at all. The slowest sample in the data has `r min(rhythm_metrics$rate)` syllables per second, so the intercept lies far outside the data. It only sets the height of the line.

:::

### 2.3 Model fit

Find `R²` with `glance()`. What does it tell you?

::: solution

```{r}
glance(m)$r.squared
```

Speech rate accounts for about `r round(100 * glance(m)$r.squared)`% of the variance in ΔC. The rest comes from everything the model leaves out: the language, the speaker, the kind of speech material and random variation.

:::

---

## 3. Predictions and residuals

### 3.1 Predictions

Which ΔC does the model predict for samples spoken at 4 and at 6 syllables per second? Use `predict()`, with the two rates in a tibble passed to `newdata`.

::: solution

```{r}
predict(m, newdata = tibble(rate = c(4, 6)))
```

Two syllables per second more means a ΔC about `r round(2 * abs(coef(m)["rate"]))` ms smaller, which is twice the slope.

:::

### 3.2 Residuals

Use `augment()` to add the [fitted values]{.hl} and the [residuals]{.hl} to the data. Plot the residuals (`.resid`) against the fitted values (`.fitted`) and add a horizontal line at 0 with `geom_hline()`. Are the residuals spread evenly around 0?

::: solution

```{r residuals, eval = FALSE}
augment(m) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum2", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  xlab("Fitted ΔC (ms)") + ylab("Residual (ms)")
```

:::

::: solution

```{r, ref.label = "residuals", echo = FALSE}
```

The residuals scatter around 0 with about the same spread across the fitted values, with no curve or funnel.

:::

### 3.3 Bonus: a hidden group

Draw the scatterplot again, with the points coloured by `material` and one line per material: `geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)`. Are the lines within each material steeper or shallower than the line of `m`?

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
rhythm_metrics |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = delta_c, colour = material)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  xlab("Speech rate (syllables per second)") + ylab("ΔC (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

:::

::: {.solution .smaller}

```{r}
rhythm_metrics |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(delta_c ~ rate))[2], .by = material)
```

All the lines within a material are shallower than the line of `m`, with its slope of `r round(coef(m)["rate"], 1)` ms per syllable per second. Sentences built from simple syllables are read fastest and have few consonant clusters, so they have a small ΔC; spontaneous speech is slowest and has a large ΔC. Across materials, these differences add to the effect of rate. In the simulation, ΔC falls by 6 ms per syllable per second (`?rhythm_metrics`). Lectures 6 and 7 show how to put both predictors in one model.

:::

### 3.4 Bonus: R² by hand

`R²` compares the residuals of `m` with those of an [intercept-only model]{.hl}, `delta_c ~ 1`, which predicts the mean ΔC for every sample. Fit it and compute `R²` by hand as 1 minus the sum of the squared residuals of `m`, divided by the sum of the squared residuals of the intercept-only model. Do you get the same number as `glance()`?

::: solution

```{r}
m0 <- lm(delta_c ~ 1, data = rhythm_metrics)
1 - sum(residuals(m)^2) / sum(residuals(m0)^2)
glance(m)$r.squared
```

The two numbers are the same.

:::
